etymology: From the Latin praevenire, “to come before, to go before” (prae, “before,” + venire, “to come”); hence to anticipate, to go before, to meet beforehand. The modern sense “to stop, to hinder” is a later drift; in the KJV to prevent is to precede.
biblical_def: To prevent, in the Authorized Version, is not to stop a thing but to go before it — to come first, to anticipate, to meet beforehand. The modern ear hears “prevent” and thinks of hindering, but the older sense is the plain Latin: to come before. Paul comforts the Thessalonians about their dead with it: “we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep” (1Th 4:15) — the living shall not go before the dead into glory, for the dead in Christ shall rise first. The psalmist uses it of prayer that outruns the dawn: “I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried: I hoped in thy word” (Psa 119:147), and again, “in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee” (Psa 88:13) — the saint’s cry rising before the sun. But the sweetest use is of God’s grace, which always comes first: “The God of my mercy shall prevent me” (Psa 59:10). Here is the whole doctrine of preventing grace — grace that goes before, that seeks the sinner ere he seeks, that loves first. We love Him because He first loved us. The Reformed faith rests on a God who prevents: who chose before the foundation, who calls before we come, who works the willing and the doing. To be prevented by such grace is to be met on the road before we knew to look for Him.
webster_summary: To go before; to anticipate; to precede — not, as now, to hinder.
webster_full: PREVENT, to go before; to precede; to anticipate; to be beforehand with.
From Latin prae (“before”) and venire (“to come”).
The modern sense, “to hinder, to stop,” is a later hardening of the word.
The living shall not prevent the dead at Christ’s coming (1Th 4:15).
God’s preventing grace goes before the sinner: He shall prevent me (Psa 59:10).
scriptures: For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep.
I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried: I hoped in thy word.
But unto thee have I cried, O LORD; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee.
The God of my mercy shall prevent me: God shall let me see my desire upon mine enemies.
corruption_summary: An old word for going before; it recovers preventing grace — the God who seeks and loves the sinner first.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift here is total: the modern reader hears “prevent” and thinks of stopping or hindering, the very opposite of the AV’s “go before.” A man who does not know it will read “we shall not prevent them which are asleep” as though Paul feared the living might obstruct the dead, when he means the living shall not precede them — the sleeping saints rise first. The reversal is worth marking wherever the word stands, for it turns comfort into confusion. To prevent the dawn is to rise before it; to have one’s prayer prevent the LORD is to cry to Him early; and to be prevented with the blessings of goodness is to be met by mercy before one asks.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is preventing grace — the doctrine buried in this vanished sense of the word. Grace prevents: it goes before. The sinner does not seek God and find grace waiting as his reward; grace seeks the sinner and finds him dead. “The God of my mercy shall prevent me,” sang David, and every saint says amen, for we love Him because He first loved us. Election prevents the will, the effectual call prevents the coming, and the blood was shed while we were yet enemies. The whole Reformed confession is compressed in this old verb: God is beforehand with His people at every step, and the crown is set on a head that grace crowned before it stooped to be saved.
roots_summary: The word means to go before, to precede, to anticipate — not to hinder.
roots_lines: Prevent — Latin praevenire, “to come before.”
From prae (“before”) + venire (“to come”).
The KJV sense is to precede or anticipate, never to hinder.
The living shall not prevent the sleeping saints (1Th 4:15).
God’s grace prevents the sinner, going before him (Psa 59:10).
usage: To prevent in the KJV is to go before: “I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried.”
The living shall not prevent them which are asleep — the dead in Christ rise first.
Preventing grace goes before the sinner: the God of mercy prevents him ere he seeks.

etymology: From two Old English verbs fallen together: lætan, “to allow,” and lettan, “to hinder, to obstruct” (kin to late). The KJV’s “let” is this second word — to hinder, to restrain — the exact opposite of the modern “let.”
biblical_def: Here is a word turned clean about. In modern English to let is to allow; in the Authorized Version to let is to hinder, to restrain, to hold back. The two senses are two different Old English verbs that wore down to the same spelling, and only the older survives in law, where a “let or hindrance” still means an obstruction, and in tennis, where a “let” is a ball hindered by the net. Scripture uses the older sense throughout. Paul tells the Romans he had often purposed to come to them, “but was let hitherto” (Rom 1:13) — hindered, prevented from coming, not permitted. Pharaoh charges Moses and Aaron, “wherefore do ye… let the people from their works?” (Exo 5:4) — why do ye hinder them from their labour? The most weighty use is prophetic: of the mystery of iniquity Paul writes, “only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way” (2Th 2:7) — there is a Restrainer who holds back the man of sin, and lawlessness cannot break loose until that hindering hand is lifted. Set against every human hindrance stands the LORD, whom none can hinder: “I will work, and who shall let it?” (Isa 43:13). There is the comfort. Men are let and hindered at every turn, their best purposes obstructed; but God is never let. His counsel shall stand, His work goes forward, and no power in heaven or earth can restrain the hand that upholds all things.
webster_summary: To hinder; to restrain; to obstruct — the reverse of the modern “to allow.”
webster_full: LET, to hinder; to obstruct; to interpose an impediment; to restrain.
From Old English lettan, “to hinder,” kin to late; distinct from lætan, “to allow.”
It survives in the legal phrase “let or hindrance” and in the game of tennis.
Paul was let — hindered — from coming to Rome (Rom 1:13).
The Restrainer letteth the man of sin until He be taken away (2Th 2:7).
scriptures: For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.
Rom 1:13
Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles.
Yea, before the day was I am he; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand: I will work, and who shall let it?
Exo 5:4
And the king of Egypt said unto them, Wherefore do ye, Moses and Aaron, let the people from their works? get you unto your burdens.
corruption_summary: An old word for hindering; it recovers the Restrainer who holds back iniquity, and the LORD whom none can hinder.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is a true reversal, and it is the most treacherous of the false friends, for the word has come to mean its own opposite. To the modern ear “let” means to permit; in the KJV it means to prevent. A reader who does not know it will take “he who now letteth will let” to mean he who now permits will permit, and lose the whole doctrine of restraint that Paul is teaching. Only the older sense makes sense of the sentence: Someone is hindering the man of sin, and will go on hindering him, until He is taken out of the way. The lawful reader must hold the two lets apart and take the harder, older one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of the Restrainer. The mystery of iniquity is already at work, held in check by a hindering power; when that power withdraws, the lawless one is revealed. Whatever the Restrainer be — the Spirit striving, the preached gospel, lawful magistracy under God — the point stands: evil is not loose in the world to the full of its will, but bridled by a hand it cannot see. And the same hand that lets the wicked cannot itself be let. “I will work, and who shall let it?” No devil hinders God; the God who hinders devils works His whole pleasure unopposed.
roots_summary: The word means to hinder, to restrain, to obstruct — not to allow.
roots_lines: Let — Old English lettan, “to hinder,” kin to late.
It is a different verb from lætan, “to allow,” though spelled alike.
The KJV sense is to obstruct or restrain, the reverse of the modern word.
Paul was let — hindered — from coming to Rome (Rom 1:13).
None can let the work of the LORD: “who shall let it?” (Isa 43:13).
usage: To let in the KJV is to hinder: Paul “was let hitherto” from coming to Rome.
He who now letteth will let — the Restrainer hinders iniquity till he be removed.
“I will work, and who shall let it?” — no power hinders the hand of God.

etymology: From the Latin conversari, “to turn oneself about, to dwell, to live among” (con- + versari, “to be turned”); hence one’s whole manner of living and dealing among men. The narrowing to mere talk is a later drift; the KJV means conduct.
biblical_def: Conversation in the Authorized Version is not talk. It is a man’s whole manner of life — his conduct, his walk, his behaviour, the sum of how he lives and deals among men. The Latin behind it means to turn oneself about among others, to dwell, to have one’s daily converse; and so the KJV can command a thing no one could command of mere speech: “let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ” (Php 1:27) — let your living match the gospel. Peter grounds it in the character of God: “as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1Pe 1:15) — not holy in your talk merely, but in every department of your conduct. Paul can speak of his former conduct in the same word: “ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God” (Gal 1:13). That was no manner of speaking; it was a manner of life spent in fury against the saints. And the believer’s true home shapes the whole of it: “our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour” (Php 3:20) — our citizenship, our commonwealth, the polity to which our lives belong, is above. Here is sanctification in one old word. A holy conversation is not smooth religious speech but a life visibly conformed to Christ, ordered by heaven’s laws while the feet still tread the earth. Men shall know the tree by more than its leaves; they shall know it by its walk.
webster_summary: One’s whole manner of life and conduct among men — not, as now, mere talk.
webster_full: CONVERSATION, general course of manners; behaviour; deportment; manner of living.
From Latin conversari, “to live among, to have dealings with.”
The narrowing to spoken discourse is a later and lesser sense of the word.
Paul’s conversation in time past was persecuting the church (Gal 1:13).
The believer’s conversation is in heaven, whence he looks for Christ (Php 3:20).
scriptures: Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;
Gal 1:13
For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews' religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it:
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: An old word for conduct; it recovers that holiness is a manner of life, not a manner of speech.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift here has cost the church dearly, for it has hidden a command in plain sight. When Peter says, “be ye holy in all manner of conversation,” the modern reader hears an exhortation to clean talk — no coarse jesting, no gossip — and while that is true and good, it is a fraction of the meaning. The word reaches the whole of a man’s conduct: his business, his marriage, his temper, his use of money and of time, his walk in the dark where no man sees. To collapse “conversation” into speech is to let nine-tenths of the command slip, and to imagine a man may be holy in his mouth while his life goes unreformed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel commands a life. “Let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ” — the good news is to be adorned not by eloquence but by conduct, a walk that fits the doctrine. This is the doctrine of sanctification pressed into a single word: the called are to be holy in all manner of their living, because the God who called them is holy. And the spring of it is heavenly citizenship. The believer’s conversation is in heaven; his life is governed by the laws of a country he has not yet seen, and it is by that strange, upward-ordered walk that the world takes knowledge of him.
roots_summary: The word means one’s whole manner of life and conduct — not merely speech.
roots_lines: Conversation — Latin conversari, “to live among.”
It means the whole course of one’s conduct and deportment.
The KJV never uses it for mere talk, but for manner of life.
Holiness is required in all manner of conversation (1Pe 1:15).
The saint’s conversation, his citizenship, is in heaven (Php 3:20).
usage: Conversation in the KJV is conduct: “be ye holy in all manner of conversation.”
Paul’s conversation in time past was persecuting the church — a life, not a speech.
Our conversation is in heaven: the whole walk is ordered by a country above.

etymology: From the Latin communicare, “to share, to make common, to impart” (from communis, “common”); hence to give a share of what one has to another. The modern narrowing to the exchange of words or information is later; the KJV means to share goods.
biblical_def: To communicate, in the Authorized Version, is not to converse but to share — to make common, to impart of one’s substance to another’s need. The Latin is plain: from communis, “common,” to communicate is to bring a thing into the common stock, to give a portion of what you have. So the word is nearly always about money, food, and material help. Paul lays a duty on the taught: “let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things” (Gal 6:6) — let the hearer share his goods with his minister. He thanks the Philippians for exactly this: “ye did communicate with my affliction” (Php 4:14) — ye shared it, ye sent relief. He binds it upon the rich: “that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate” (1Ti 6:18) — open-handed, free to share. And he ranks such giving among the sacrifices of God: “to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” (Heb 13:16). Here is a whole grace hidden in a faded word. The primitive church had all things common by this very spirit — every man reckoning his goods a common stock for his brother’s need. To communicate is worship: the open hand is a sacrifice, and God smells a sweet savour in the loaf broken for the hungry and the coin loosed for the poor. He that hath this world’s good and shutteth up his bowels does not communicate, and the love of God dwelleth not in him.
webster_summary: To share; to impart of one’s substance; to give a portion to another’s need.
webster_full: COMMUNICATE, to impart; to share; to give to another a part of what one has.
From Latin communicare, from communis, “common.”
In the KJV it means chiefly to share goods, not to exchange words.
The taught are to communicate to their teacher in all good things (Gal 6:6).
To do good and to communicate is a sacrifice pleasing to God (Heb 13:16).
scriptures: Gal 6:6
Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.
Php 4:14
Notwithstanding ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction.
That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
corruption_summary: An old word for sharing goods; it recovers liberality as a sacrifice well-pleasing to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is quiet but costly. Our age has narrowed “communicate” to the traffic of words — to speak, to inform, to exchange messages — until an age that communicates ceaselessly has forgotten the older and weightier sense: to share what one owns. When Paul bids the rich be “willing to communicate,” he is not commending good conversation but an open hand. To read our sense back into the text is to turn a command about money into a command about talk, and to let the wealthy off the very duty the apostle pressed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that liberality is a sacrifice. “To do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.” The giving of goods to a brother’s need is set beside the praise of the lips as a thing offered up to God and smelled by Him as a sweet savour. The taught owe their teacher a share of their substance; the afflicted are to be relieved; the rich are to hold their wealth as a common stock ready for distribution. This is not the world’s enforced levelling, which seizes; it is charity, which gives freely from a heart the grace of God has opened. The primitive believers reckoned nothing their own because Another had first communicated all things to them, and the church that has forgotten the word has too often forgotten the deed.
roots_summary: The word means to share, to impart of one’s goods to another’s need.
roots_lines: Communicate — Latin communicare, “to make common.”
From communis, “common”; hence to give a share of one’s own.
In the KJV it means to share goods, not to exchange words.
The taught communicate to their teacher in all good things (Gal 6:6).
To communicate is a sacrifice with which God is well pleased (Heb 13:16).
usage: To communicate in the KJV is to share: “willing to communicate” means open-handed.
The Philippians did communicate with Paul’s affliction — they sent him relief.
To do good and to communicate is a sacrifice God smells as a sweet savour.

etymology: From the Latin occupare, “to seize, to take up, to employ”; in older English “to occupy” meant to trade with, to use, to put to work — to employ goods or money in business. The modern narrowing to “to fill a space” or “to dwell in” is later.
biblical_def: To occupy, in the older English of the Authorized Version, is to trade — to employ, to put to use, to do business with. The modern reader hears “occupy” and thinks of filling a room or holding a seat; the KJV means to set money and goods to work for gain. Ezekiel’s great lament over Tyre is a merchant’s ledger, and the word is everywhere in it: “they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work” (Eze 27:16); “Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs” (Eze 27:19); “they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats” (Eze 27:21) — the nations trafficking in Tyre’s markets. But the word’s home in the believer’s ear is the nobleman’s charge to his servants: he “delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come” (Luk 19:13) — not “sit and hold,” but “trade with this, put it to work, until I return.” The pound was capital; the command was industry. And the reckoning fell hardest on the man who did neither — who wrapped his pound in a napkin and kept it safe and idle, and was condemned not for losing it but for not trading with it. Here is the whole doctrine of Christian stewardship. The Master is gone into a far country and will return; every gift, hour, and talent He has left is capital lent for trade; and the servant is not to bury it in caution but to occupy — to lay it out for his Lord’s increase against the day of account.
webster_summary: To trade; to employ; to put goods or money to use in business — not merely to fill a space.
webster_full: OCCUPY, to use; to employ; to trade with; to put to business or profit.
From Latin occupare, “to seize, to take up, to employ.”
The narrowing to “fill a space” or “dwell in” is a later sense.
The nations occupied — traded — in the fairs of Tyre (Eze 27:16).
The servants were bidden, “Occupy till I come” (Luk 19:13).
scriptures: And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate.
Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs: bright iron, cassia, and calamus, were in thy market.
Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants.
corruption_summary: An old word for trading; it recovers stewardship — the Master’s capital lent to be put to work till He come.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here empties the Lord’s command of its force. “Occupy till I come” now sounds to the modern ear like “hold your position, keep the seat warm, endure until I return” — a counsel of mere waiting. It is nearly the opposite of what the nobleman said. He handed each servant capital and bade him trade with it: employ this, venture it, make it multiply. The idle reading has done real harm, breeding a Christianity of holding-ground rather than laying-out, of keeping oneself unspotted while burying every gift in a napkin. The servant so minded was the one the lord condemned.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is active stewardship under an absent and returning Lord. The pounds were not the servants’ own; they were entrusted, to be occupied — put to work — against a reckoning. So it is with every mercy God lends: strength, money, learning, opportunity, the gospel itself. He is gone into a far country to receive a kingdom and will return, and He will require His own with usury. The unprofitable servant did not squander his pound; he merely kept it safe and idle, and that was his ruin. To occupy is to refuse the napkin — to trade boldly with what the Master left, so that at His coming He may receive His own with increase.
roots_summary: The word means to trade, to employ, to put money or goods to use.
roots_lines: Occupy — Latin occupare, “to take up, to employ.”
In older English, to occupy is to trade with, to put to use.
The KJV sense is commercial, not spatial: to do business.
The nations occupied in the fairs of Tyre (Eze 27:16).
“Occupy till I come” — trade with the pound (Luk 19:13).
usage: To occupy in the KJV is to trade: the merchants occupied in the fairs of Tyre.
“Occupy till I come” means trade with the pound, not merely hold the ground.
The servant who would not occupy his pound, but hid it, was condemned as unprofitable.

etymology: From the Old French ensuivre, “to follow after” (from Latin insequi, in- + sequi, “to follow”); hence to pursue, to follow hard after. The modern intransitive sense, “to result, to follow as a consequence,” is a weakening; the KJV means to pursue.
biblical_def: To ensue, in the Authorized Version, is to pursue — to follow hard after, to chase, to give oneself in earnest to the getting of a thing. The modern ear takes “ensue” as something that merely happens next, a consequence that follows of itself: a silence ensued. But the KJV’s ensue is active and strenuous, a verb of pursuit. It stands in Peter’s counsel for a good life and good days: “let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it” (1Pe 3:11) — not wait for peace to arrive, but hunt it, run after it. Peter is quoting the Psalm, where the same command reads with the plainer verb: “seek peace, and pursue it” (Psa 34:14) — the two words are one. Paul lays the same charge on the Romans: “if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18), which is peace pursued to the very edge of what a man can do. And Hebrews binds pursuit to holiness: “follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Heb 12:14). Mark that peace and holiness are not to be awaited but chased. The believer does not drift into either. He eschews the evil that murders peace, does the good that makes it, and then runs after it as a man runs after a fleeing thing he is resolved to catch. To ensue peace is to make peace one’s pursuit — and the peacemakers, not the peace-wishers, shall be called the children of God.
webster_summary: To pursue; to follow after; to chase — not merely to follow as a result.
webster_full: ENSUE, to follow; to pursue; to follow after with intent to overtake.
From Old French ensuivre, from Latin insequi, “to follow after.”
The weakened sense, “to result, to happen next,” is a later drift.
The KJV bids the saint seek peace and ensue — pursue — it (1Pe 3:11).
The parallel psalm reads, “seek peace, and pursue it” (Psa 34:14).
scriptures: Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it.
Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
corruption_summary: An old word for pursuing; it recovers that peace and holiness are chased, not awaited.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here softens a strong command into a weak observation. In modern usage “ensue” is passive — a thing that follows on its own, as chaos ensues or a quarrel ensues — and a reader who carries that sense to 1Pe 3:11 will hear “seek peace, and ensue it” as though peace, once sought, will simply come about. Peter means no such thing. His ensue is a hunter’s word: pursue peace, run it down, do not let it escape. The passive reading breeds a passive disciple, waiting for peace and holiness to settle on him like weather, when Scripture sends him out after them like game.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pursuit of peace and holiness as a duty of the will. “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.” The word is follow — pursue, ensue — and the stakes could not be higher, for without holiness no man shall see God. Neither peace nor holiness is a mood that descends; both are a quarry the believer chases with all that lieth in him. He eschews evil, does good, and then presses after peace to the utmost edge of possibility, making peace where he can and keeping it where he cannot make it. To ensue is to be no passive Christian, but a pursuer — and grace makes such pursuers of us all.
roots_summary: The word means to pursue, to follow hard after, to chase.
roots_lines: Ensue — Old French ensuivre, from Latin insequi, “to follow after.”
It means to pursue, to chase, not merely to result.
The KJV sense is active pursuit, a hunter’s word.
Seek peace, and ensue it — pursue it (1Pe 3:11).
The psalm’s parallel: “seek peace, and pursue it” (Psa 34:14).
usage: To ensue in the KJV is to pursue: “seek peace, and ensue it.”
Peace is not awaited but chased — the peacemakers are called the children of God.
Follow peace and holiness: ensue them as a man runs down a fleeing thing.

etymology: From the Latin affectare, “to strive after, to aim at, to court” (a frequentative of afficere, “to influence”); hence to seek earnestly, to court, to be zealous toward. The modern sense, “to influence” or “to feign,” is later; the KJV means to court zealously.
biblical_def: To affect, in the Authorized Version, is to court — to seek earnestly after, to woo, to be zealous toward a person or thing. The modern reader knows “affect” only as “to influence” (the weather affects the crops) or “to feign” (to affect a manner), and both are wide of the KJV, where to affect is to pursue with warmth, to set one’s heart and effort upon. Paul uses it of the Judaizers who were courting the Galatians for ill: “they zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them” (Gal 4:17) — they woo you, they make much of you, but to shut you up to themselves. Yet the courting itself is not condemned, only its object and end; for Paul at once adds, “it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing” (Gal 4:18). The heart was made to affect, to seek earnestly; the question is only what. So he bids the Corinthians “covet earnestly the best gifts” (1Co 12:31) — affect the highest things, not the showy — and he bids the Colossians, “set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:2). Here is a doctrine of the ordered heart. Fallen man affects the wrong things zealously — money, praise, the flesh, the flattering teacher who courts him — and the cure is not a cold heart but a rightly aimed one. Grace does not quench the affections; it converts them, turning the whole earnest pursuit of the soul from things on the earth to things above, where Christ sitteth at the right hand of God.
webster_summary: To court; to seek earnestly after; to be zealous toward — not merely to influence or to feign.
webster_full: AFFECT, to aim at; to court; to seek earnestly; to be zealous toward.
From Latin affectare, “to strive after, to court.”
The senses “to influence” and “to feign” are later developments.
The Judaizers zealously affected — courted — the Galatians (Gal 4:17).
It is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing (Gal 4:18).
scriptures: Gal 4:17
They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them.
Gal 4:18
But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you.
But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.
Col 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
corruption_summary: An old word for courting or seeking earnestly; it recovers the ordered heart that affects the things above.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here has hollowed the word of its warmth. To the modern ear “affect” is either cold or false: it names one thing acting upon another, or a manner put on for show. But the KJV’s affect is the heart in ardent pursuit — to court, to woo, to seek with zeal. A reader who knows only the modern senses will miss the drama of Galatians 4, where two courtships contend for a church: the Judaizers zealously affecting the Galatians to shut them up to a false gospel, and Paul travailing in birth again until Christ be formed in them. The whole passage is about who shall win the affections, and the faded word hides the fight.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordering of the affections, not their extinction. Fallen man is not a creature of too much passion but of misdirected passion: he zealously affects money, applause, and the flesh, and courts the teacher who flatters him. The Stoic remedy is a cold heart; the gospel remedy is a converted one. “It is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing.” So Scripture does not bid us feel less but seek higher: covet earnestly the best gifts, set the affection on things above where Christ is. Grace takes the same ardour that once ran after vanity and turns it heavenward, until a man affects Christ with all the zeal he once spent on the world.
roots_summary: The word means to court, to seek earnestly, to be zealous toward.

etymology: From the Latin allegare, “to send, to adduce, to cite as proof,” crossed in older English with the legal esligier; hence to bring forward, to set forth, to cite in evidence. The modern sense, “to assert without proof,” is nearly the reverse; the KJV means to prove by citation.
biblical_def: To allege, in the Authorized Version, is to bring forth as proof — to set forth, to adduce, to cite in evidence. This is one of the sharpest of the false friends, for the modern sense runs almost backward: today an “alleged” thing is one merely asserted and not yet proven, a charge under suspicion. The KJV means the opposite — not the unproven claim but the proof itself, the citing of evidence to establish a case. It occurs once, and it describes Paul’s method in the synagogue of Thessalonica: he was “opening and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead” (Act 17:3) — opening the Scriptures and laying out from them the proof that the Messiah must die and rise. It was reasoning from a text, evidence adduced, not opinion floated. Luke describes the same labour in Apollos, who “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28), and in Paul again, who “three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2). And the LORD Himself invites the contest of proofs: “Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons” (Isa 41:21). Here is a pattern for all gospel preaching and defence. The faith is not asserted but alleged — opened out of the Scriptures and proven from them. The apostles did not merely announce that Christ was risen; they went to the Law and the Prophets and demonstrated that He must be. To allege is to lay the text on the table and let it make the case.
webster_summary: To bring forward as proof; to cite in evidence; to adduce — not to assert without proof.
webster_full: ALLEGE, to produce as an argument or plea; to cite; to adduce in proof.

corruption_summary: An old word for citing proof; it recovers preaching that is opened and proven out of the Scriptures.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is a near-reversal worth pausing over. In the courtroom and the newspaper of our day, to allege is to charge without having proven — the “alleged” offender, the “alleged” fact, the claim held at arm’s length until evidence arrives. The KJV’s allege is the evidence itself. When Paul goes “opening and alleging” that Christ must suffer and rise, he is not floating an untested theory; he is laying out proof from the text of Scripture, demonstrating from Moses and the Prophets what the Messiah must be. To carry the modern sense into Acts 17 is to imagine Paul merely asserting where in fact he was proving.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the evidential character of gospel preaching. The apostles did not preach by bare assertion or by appeal to their own authority; they alleged — they opened the Scriptures and adduced them as proof. Paul reasoned three sabbath days out of the Scriptures; Apollos mightily convinced the Jews, shewing by the Scriptures that Jesus was Christ. The pattern rebukes both a preaching that merely emotes and a defence of the faith that merely opines. The faith stands on evidence God has given, and the LORD Himself throws down the challenge: “Produce your cause… bring forth your strong reasons.” To allege Christ is to set the sacred text upon the table and let the Word of God prove the Son of God.

etymology: From the Latin convincere, “to overcome, to refute, to prove guilty” (con- intensive + vincere, “to conquer”); hence to convict, to prove wrong, to overcome by argument. The modern narrowing to “persuade of a truth” loses the note of guilt; the KJV means to convict.
biblical_def: To convince, in the Authorized Version, is to convict — to overcome by argument, to refute, to prove a man wrong and guilty. The Latin is convincere, to conquer utterly; and the KJV’s convince keeps the sterner edge that our softer “persuade” has lost. To convince a man is not merely to bring him round to your opinion, but to overpower his defence and leave him without answer — often to prove him a sinner. So the Lord Jesus flings the challenge, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Joh 8:46) — which of you can prove Me guilty of one? None could. When the accusers of the adulteress heard His word, they “being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one” (Joh 8:9) — the same conquering work, done inwardly by conscience. James says the respecter of persons is “convinced of the law as transgressors” (Jas 2:9) — proven guilty, condemned by the very law he thought to keep. And the elder must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — not to charm them but to stop their mouths, to refute the contradiction and lay the error bare. Here is a word the church needs back. The office of the Word is not only to comfort but to convict; the Spirit is come to reprove the world of sin. Before a man is persuaded of the gospel he must first be convinced of his guilt — conquered, silenced, shut up under sin — that he may flee to the Christ whom none could convince of any.
webster_summary: To convict; to refute; to prove wrong or guilty; to overcome by argument — not merely to persuade.
webster_full: CONVINCE, to convict; to refute; to prove guilty; to overpower by argument.
From Latin convincere, “to overcome, to refute.”
The KJV keeps the note of guilt the modern “persuade” has lost.

corruption_summary: An old word for convicting; it recovers the Word’s work of proving men guilty and shutting their mouths.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here has softened a hard and necessary word. In modern speech to convince a man is simply to bring him to agree — a matter of persuasion, of winning him over, with no thought of guilt. The KJV’s convince is a verdict, not a preference: to convince is to convict, to refute, to prove a man wrong and leave him without a plea. When Christ says, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” He is not asking who disagrees with Him but who can prove Him guilty. To read the mild modern sense into these texts is to lose the courtroom in them, and to imagine the gospel merely woos the mind when in fact it first arraigns the conscience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is conviction of sin. The Spirit is come to reprove — to convince — the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment; and no man is savingly persuaded of Christ who has not first been convinced of his guilt. The accusers of the adulteress were convicted by their own conscience and went out one by one; the respecter of persons is convinced of the law as a transgressor; the gainsayer is to be convinced by sound doctrine and his mouth stopped. A ministry that only comforts and never convicts has kept half the Word’s office and lost the sharper half. Grace does not flatter the sinner into heaven; it convinces him of sin, that he may flee to the sinless One whom none could convince of any.

etymology: From the Latin translatus, “carried across” (past participle of transferre, “to carry over”); hence to bear across, to transfer, to remove from one place or state to another. The narrowing to the rendering of words from one tongue to another is a later and lesser sense.
biblical_def: To translate, in the Authorized Version, is to carry across — to transfer, to remove bodily from one place or state to another. The modern reader thinks first of turning words from one language into another, but that is a late and narrow use; the KJV’s translate is a verb of removal, a bearing-over of persons and kingdoms. Abner swears to translate the kingdom “from the house of Saul” and to set up David’s throne (2Sa 3:10) — to carry the crown across from one house to another. Enoch was translated bodily out of this life: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him” (Heb 11:5) — caught away, removed, borne across the river of death without passing through it. But the word’s glory is in Paul’s gospel, where it describes what God has done to every believer: He “hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son” (Col 1:13). Mark the two kingdoms and the carrying-over between them. The Christian has not been coaxed to change sides; he has been seized out of the dominion of darkness and transferred, a whole man, into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love. This is the language of that other word to Paul — “to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18). Regeneration is a translation. The sinner does not migrate by degrees; he is carried across in a moment by sovereign grace, from death to life, from Satan’s realm to Christ’s.
webster_summary: To carry across; to transfer; to remove from one place or state to another — not merely to render into another tongue.
webster_full: TRANSLATE, to bear across; to remove or transfer from one place or condition to another.
From Latin transferre, “to carry over,” participle translatus.
The sense of rendering words from one language to another is a later narrowing.
Enoch was translated that he should not see death (Heb 11:5).
God hath translated believers into the kingdom of His Son (Col 1:13).

corruption_summary: An old word for carrying across; it recovers regeneration as a translation out of darkness into the kingdom of the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is a narrowing rather than a reversal, but it is real. Our first thought at “translate” is of language — the rendering of a text from Greek into English — and that sense, though good, is small beside the KJV’s. There translate is to carry a thing bodily across: a crown from Saul’s house to David’s, Enoch out of life without dying, a sinner from one kingdom into another. A reader who hears only the linguistic sense will miss the sheer physical force of Col 1:13, where God does not merely teach or persuade the sinner but lifts and carries him out of the domain of darkness altogether.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the monergism of the new birth. To be saved is to be translated — carried across — and the verb has no room for the sinner’s own legs. God “hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son”: the deliverance and the translation are His act, done to a man who was under the power of darkness and could not walk himself out. Regeneration is not a decision that migrates a man by inches but a sovereign removal that bears him over in a moment, from death to life, from Satan’s realm to Christ’s. As Enoch was not found because God had taken him, so the believer is not found in the old kingdom, because God has carried him into the new.
